placeholders.days: whole days since the relevant event — the student's last visit, a past failure on this problem, or the length of the current unbroken practice streak
placeholders.streak: number of consecutive correct drills in the current run
placeholders.attempts: how many attempts the student previously needed on this problem
placeholders.secret: the name of the secret currently being taught or tested
placeholders.idiom: the C++ expression at the heart of the current secret
placeholders.requirement: name of the gate dimension that is short: recognition, understanding, implementation, or retention
placeholders.shortfall: how far the short gate dimension sits below its threshold, as a percentage
placeholders.score: how many final-test problems were answered correctly
placeholders.total: number of problems in the final test
placeholders.required: how many must be answered correctly to pass

greeting_first: Sit. How many paths join n glades, if every glade can be reached and none can be reached twice? Say the number aloud. Everything I teach you follows from it.
You have come to the wood. Before anything else: which glade is the root? Nobody will ever tell you. Does that trouble you, and should it?

Other masters will show you a technique and ask you to repeat it. I am going to ask you questions until you say the technique yourself. You may find that slower. Ask yourself why I would choose it anyway.
What is a visited array for? Answer that honestly and half of this region is already yours.
greeting_returning: Again. What does a recursive call give you the instant it returns, that you did not have before it?
Sit. Which direction does today's question look — downwards into what a glade commands, or upwards towards what commands it?
You came back. Good. Then: how many numbers must a child send to its parent, and what decides that?
Continue. Where does the combining line go, and why is there only one place it can go?
greeting_after_gap: {days} days. Tell me without looking: what replaces the visited array here, and why is it enough?
Gone {days} days. The wood did not move. Has the answer to 'which glade is the top' changed while you were away?
{days} days. A centre worth 3 with three leaves worth 2 each. What does taking the best glade first score? Start there and the rest will come back.
{days} days away. Which of the two loops goes on the outside when you build the jump table? If you had to think, we begin one stage earlier.
lesson_intro: {secret}. Before I show you anything — what is the question the statement is actually asking? Say it in one sentence with no code in it.
One walk. Watch what it folds, not how it moves. Can you tell me in advance which of those two ever changes between problems?
I will give you a wood and a rule. You will tell me what a glade must report to its parent. Ready?
This one is short. So ask the useful question first: what would go wrong if you did the obvious thing instead?
lesson_memorise: Keep `{idiom}`. Not because it is clever — ask yourself how many of this region's problems end at that one line.
Learn it until you no longer have to derive it. Then, when it fails you, you will notice — which is the only reason memorising is worth anything.
Take it now. Under a clock, will you rederive this, or will you type it?
In the hand. And the reason it works — where does that go, and how would you prove you still had it?
drill_correct: That is it. Hold on to how you got there.
drill_wrong: No. You went back the way you came. What was supposed to stop you?
Wrong. You read the child's value — but had it been computed yet?
No. You took every child. The longest walk bends once; how many branches meet at the bend?
Wrong. You summed the children's skipped values. If the parent is empty, what is the child forbidden from doing?
No. That product was computed in int. What is the largest it can be when n is two hundred thousand?
Wrong. You jumped when the two landed on the same glade. What was the loop trying to avoid?
No. You read the answer off the root. Must the longest walk touch the root at all?
drill_streak: {streak} in a row. The hand is quick. Is the reason arriving with it, or after it?
{streak} straight. Now tell me one of them again, slower, and say why.
Good rhythm. What happens to it when I take the labels off?
trial_intro: Nothing named. First question: how many places, how many links, and can you get from any one to any other?
Read it twice. What is the answer asked about — one glade, every glade, or a pair of them?
One problem. Before you write anything: does the question look downwards or upwards?
The label is off. The constraints are not. What does the bound on n forbid you from doing?
fail_wrong_pattern: No. Were both ends of that route given to you, or were you asked to find them? Answer that and you had the right technique in front of you.
Wrong tool. Did any choice at one place forbid a choice at another? If nothing was forbidden, why did you carry a state?
No. That question was about everything below a place, not about the route between two of them. Which direction were you looking?
That was one number per place, not two. What would the parent have needed to know that a single total could not tell it?
No. Count the links again. n links, not n-1 — so what did your parent guard fail to stop?
fail_timeout: Time. You knew it was a wood in the first minute. What were you doing for the rest of it?
Time ran out. Nothing you had was wrong; it was slow. Is that a knowing problem or a typing problem?
Time. You answered it once per glade, did you not? What would one walk have cost?
Time. Nothing is lost. Which part took longest — deciding, or writing?
fail_wrong_answer: The walk was right. Where was the combining line — above the recursive call, or below it?
Right idea. The product overflowed. How large is s times (n - s) when n is two hundred thousand, and what type was it in?
Close. You kept the deepest branch. How many do you need to glue a walk together?
The states were right and one transition was not. If the parent is left empty, is the child forbidden anything at all?
Correct approach. It died on one test. What shape was that test, and how deep did your recursion go?
You levelled the two glades and then ran the loop anyway. What if levelling had already made them equal?
success: Correct. Say the reason once, then move on.
Done. The next one gives less away.
success_fast: Quick — and you counted the links before you counted anything else. That is the right order.
You asked which direction it looked before you asked which technique. Good.
No wasted structure. Did you know it was a fold, or did you find out?
Fast. Now: could you have said why in the same time?
praise_exceptional: That was well done. You found the case where the root has one child before I could ask about it.
You refused the greedy and produced the four-glade wood that refutes it. Few students produce the counterexample; most only accept one.
You asked what the parent needed to know, and the number of states fell out. That is the question, and you asked it unprompted.
That is the best you have done here. You did not recall a technique. You derived one, and then recognised it.
praise_major: I have asked a great many students what a visited array is for. Most answer correctly and still write one. You stopped writing them, and you can say why. You have earned my respect.
You arrived able to walk a wood. You leave able to say what a glade must tell its parent, and to count how many numbers that takes, on a problem neither of us has seen. You have earned my respect.
I do not say this often and will not repeat it: you no longer ask me which technique. You ask the statement, and it answers you. You have earned my respect.
memorisation_detected: You produce the right line and cannot say what the parent needed. Are those the same thing? A different problem, then.
You pass the woods you have seen and fail their variants. What have you actually retained — the fold, or the file?
Change the rule from 'no two adjacent' to 'three dyes, neighbours differ' and you stall. How many states does the second one need, and why could you not derive it?
improvement_noticed: You failed this {days} days ago. Today you asked the right question first. Do you notice which one it was?
You needed {attempts} attempts on this once. Today, one. What changed — the technique, or the question you opened with?
This is the problem where you rooted at glade 1 and read the answer off it. You did not do that today.
Straighter than last time. You counted the links before you chose anything.
commitment_noticed: {days} days unbroken. Do you know how many students leave when I answer a question with a question?
Most who reach this wood want to be told. You keep coming back to be asked. That is rarer, and it is the half I cannot teach.
You have returned after every failure so far. I keep count. Should I keep counting?
Talent walks in here weekly and leaves the moment the first answer is another question. You did not.
gate_locked: Not yet. {requirement} is short by {shortfall} percent. What would you do differently if I let you through today?
The gate holds. Understanding is short — you can write the fold. Can you say what a glade reports and why one number would not do?
No. Recognition is short. Given a statement, can you yet tell me whether it looks downwards or upwards? That is the whole of it.
Implementation is short. You know where the combining line goes. Do your hands?
Retention is short. Which of the six could you still write without me? Go and find out; that is the review.
gate_open: Nothing is short. Do you feel ready, or merely permitted? Both are acceptable answers.
The gate is open. When would you like to walk through it?
You meet the requirements. The rest is your judgement, and it is time you used it.
final_test_intro: I will name nothing. Every question I have asked you was so that I would not have to. What is the first thing you check on each statement?
{total} problems, {required} of them right. For each, three questions — how many links, which direction, and how many numbers does a child owe its parent.
No help. Only statements. Which of them are you expecting to be a fold?
Some of these look upwards and some look down. Nothing will tell you which. What will?
victory: It is done. Tell me — which question turned out to be the one that mattered?
You passed. Remember that you were never given a root, and that it never mattered. Go.
Finished. Everything after this branches worse and asks the same three questions. You have them.
That is mastery of the wood. The sea is next, and nothing there has unique routes. What breaks first, do you think?
